items.title: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Yeah, and I was sick, and the day of the recording date, I was out of it, so I called Quincy [Jones] and he conducted for me, but all of the arrangements are mine – almost all of them.

ctx.x: That flavor of your writing for strings sounds like something I’ve heard on one of her albums, and you have written for Dinah. What – Gloria approached you about writing?
Yeah, and I was sick, and the day of the recording date, I was out of it, so I called Quincy [Jones] and he conducted for me, but all of the arrangements are mine – almost all of them.

items.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: they saw the Quincy Jones band and they saw Melba writing – what is it? Reverie. That she had done the arrangement on.

ctx.x: I never even thought twice about it. Can she play? That’s all I care. Can she play? Clora Bryant I met when I was 12 years old. She was with Sweethearts of Rhythm. You know Clora? Trumpet player. 12 years old. Please. Can she play? That’s all. Whatever it is. I don’t care.

It opened the door for Diva and so many of these other things. When I talk to Ellen Seeling and those people, they tell me, the first time they saw it was when they saw the Quincy Jones band and they saw Melba writing – what is it? Reverie. That she had done the arrangement on.
